quotes.quote: Now, the inability of the city to manage expenses down to this inflation level, given its massive purchasing power, a stagnant population, ever-increasing property values, as we all know, and, well, a bazillion dollars' worth of entertainment stuff, I just can't understand why they can't handle that. At some point, the fiscal irresponsibility has to end.
quotes.why: A resident argues the proposed FY 2025 budget grows well beyond inflation despite the city's purchasing power and rising property values, voicing opposition as the council adopted the budget.

quotes.quote: May the budget reflect the moral priorities of our city to keep it safe and flourishing.
quotes.why: In the opening invocation, a member of the clergy frames the evening's budget decisions as a question of the city's moral priorities.

quotes.quote: We should also caution the council that all these public discussions about decreased revenue could cause unintended consequences. Namely, citizens setting their citations for a jury trial, hiring an attorney, and making the argument, although they made a traffic violation, that the city's public comments, recordings, news articles regarding citation revenue may provide enough reasonable doubt in just one juror's mind as to why the citation was issued.
quotes.why: A police association representative warns that public discussion of declining citation revenue could give cited drivers grounds for reasonable doubt at jury trials.

quotes.quote: I was wanting to ask you, doesn't everyone have to be somewhere? We have a terrible problem with homeless people here, and no one even seems to acknowledge it, especially the police department.
quotes.why: A resident tells the council that homelessness in the city goes unacknowledged and criticizes how police treat homeless people.

quotes.quote: And during that process in the spring, if they move forward after tonight from City Council, then the developers will be looking at their zoning changes if necessary, and all three of these would require a zoning change.
quotes.why: Staff tells council that each of the three affordable housing projects would require a rezoning before it could proceed.

quotes.quote: if someone has a warrant for their arrest on a municipal court, you know, through our municipal court, they will not be arrested when they go in. We want people to be able to come in, take care of that business without fear of being arrested.
quotes.why: Staff describes the municipal court's safe harbor practice during the warrant clearance drive running through March 13.

quotes.quote: we've been funding for arch and cultural brick and mortar. You need to be in the cultural and tourism district and really have brick and mortar, but there's a need for programming and groups to have some funding.
quotes.why: A council member describes the debate over directing hotel occupancy tax dollars to brick-and-mortar institutions versus programming groups.

quotes.quote: Last year, traffic stops increased 24% as compared to 2024, and that is over 20,000 additional traffic stops. As a consequence, it resulted in a 14% decrease in fatality crashes in Arlington in 2025 as compared to 2024.
quotes.why: The patrol bureau commander links the council-backed increase in traffic enforcement to a drop in fatal crashes.

quotes.quote: my belief is those that can pay the fare rate pay the fare rate. Those that can't, we should supplement more. We are not, by federal law, allowed to do a variable rate based on income.
quotes.why: A council member explained why an income-based fare option was not legally available before voting to approve the increase.

quotes.quote: I would like the opportunity to present a comparison of city tax revenue based on land use you can all then collectively make an informed decision on how to best steward vacant land in Arlington in a way that is holistic and fiscally responsible
quotes.why: The applicant's representative argued the council should weigh tax revenue by land use before deciding the rezoning.

quotes.quote: For the on-demand service, the average cost to provide each ride is around $17 right now.
quotes.why: A transportation staff member quantified the substantial per-ride subsidy behind the proposed fare increase.

quotes.quote: our HOA alone by ourselves cannot control upstream flow we cannot modify city infrastructure we cannot slow water that is released in our neighborhood from outside our boundaries yet we are the ones living with the consequences
quotes.why: A resident argued the neighborhood could not fix stormwater damage without city engineering leadership because the problem originates in public infrastructure.

quotes.quote: There were no enforcement mechanisms in that ordinance. Let me repeat that. There were none.
quotes.why: A council member responded to claims that the previous ordinance offered enforceable protections.

quotes.quote: The city of Arlington has no local laws against discrimination. Victims of discrimination will be given a phone number to a federal agency to file a formal complaint, if applicable.
quotes.why: A resident proposed city marketing language that would state the ordinance's practical effect.

quotes.quote: Leaving the ordinance permanently suspended would mean telling our residents, our workers, our families, our visitors, that Arlington has nothing on the books, affirming fair treatment and equal access.
quotes.why: The mayor described the consequences of allowing the anti-discrimination ordinance to remain suspended.

quotes.quote: This would be a fantastic resolution, and it would be a great statement of who we are as a city if it had not come 35 seconds after stripping Arlington residents of their basic civil rights. The words are great, the thoughts are great, but it is done on the heels of taking away civil rights.
quotes.why: A commenter argues that the resolution's message is undercut by the council's earlier action.

quotes.quote: if we did it in the May election, we could get that overturned with as little as like 8,000 or 9,000 voters voting in favor of the new three-year term limits. Because I don't think any of y'all are currently serving with more than 11,000 votes in your favor.
quotes.why: A commenter argues placing the charter change on the November ballot rather than May affects how many votes it would take to change term limits.

quotes.quote: In fact, over 60,000 people wanted strict term limits and voted for it. And I really when you maybe drive home think about 60,000. Start counting from 1 to 60,000. It's a lot of people.
quotes.why: A resident who campaigned for the 2018 term limits argues the large vote shows council should not revisit them.

quotes.quote: APD currently has 706 sworn positions and currently we have 43 vacancies. This puts us at 663 officers to service 397,000 citizens in the city of Arlington. We currently have 246 officers assigned to patrol the four districts within the city. That is the same number we have had on patrol since 2008.
quotes.why: A police association board member uses staffing figures to argue patrol numbers have not kept pace with population growth.

quotes.quote: I'm telling you, six years you can't learn this job. There's no way you can learn this job. There's so much to it than that.
quotes.why: The mayor argues longer terms are needed because six years is too short to master the council's work.

quotes.quote: The existing restrictions on multifamily residential and certain retail were intended to limit development intensity and reduce impacts associated with increased traffic, wastewater, stormwater runoff, and pollutants, such as oil grease, fertilizers, and even pet waste.
quotes.why: A commenter urges council to protect the aquifer recharge zone by rejecting increased residential density in Circle C.

quotes.quote: Right now, city code only requires AEDs in buildings over 75 feet tall, but my pastor didn't collapse in a high-rise. Most people don't. It could be a dad at the gym, a grandmother at a grocery store, or a kid on a soccer field on a Saturday morning.
quotes.why: A commenter advocates expanding municipal requirements for automated external defibrillators into ordinary community spaces.

quotes.quote: This proposal for a six-story, approximately 435-unit apartment complex, we've been told that could mean 2,000 vehicle trips daily on a small residential street without sidewalks.
quotes.why: A resident voices neighborhood concern over vehicle traffic and lack of sidewalks surrounding the proposed school redevelopment.

quotes.quote: Although the zoning tract is 67 acres, the entirety of track 10 is 190 acres. That means with 16 acres of developable land, we have over 173 acres of property that will not be developed.
quotes.why: The applicant's representative outlines the limited development footprint and preserved open space for Tract 110.

items.T1: Funding in the amount of $93,000 would provide for the addition of two custodial staff for the library. The current level of staffing is inadequate to meet the demands of cleaning 23 high-activity facilities seven days a week. The addition of these two custodians will minimize on sanitary conditions, ensuring the health and safety of our customers and staff. The library is currently involved in four ongoing CIP projects. As I mentioned before, there is growing anticipation for the new central library for the future, which will incorporate such unique elements as outdoor reading porches, rooftop garden, bicycle corral, state-of-the-art technology, and many public meeting spaces. Currently, the design development phase is underway and 60% design schematics is anticipated to be completed in September of 2012. We estimate that all exterior security cameras will be operational by the end of the fiscal year. The wastewater line replacement project at the History Center has reached the end of design development phase to be completed also by the end of the fiscal year. And the John Henry Fox Central Library boiler and flue retrofit has completed the preliminary design phase.
items.T2: with Austin Energy to check out wattmeter devices at every library to measure how much electricity plug-ins draw from the power grid. All 50 wattmeters are checked out continuously. This next slide highlights outcomes of our key performance measures in 2011. The library exceeded or remained constant in nearly every measure and only slightly decreased in one. Materials expenditures increased 21% from fiscal year 2010, but we still remain just above the lower quartile for our peer libraries, and we lag behind the average for peer libraries. Circulation per capita increased 5% from the previous year, but falls below the average of peer libraries. Visits per capita decreased 6% from 2010, but keep in mind that the Southeast Austin Library was closed during fiscal year 2010, from December 2010 through September 2011, for an extensive renovation project. Program attendance per capita decreased by one-tenth of a percent, also due to the closure of the Southeast Austin branch. Citizen satisfaction of materials increased by 1%, 72% of responding citizens, and citizen satisfaction with quality of city libraries remained constant. This next slide shows the satisfaction ratings for the specific library services assessed as part of the city's annual community survey. Cleanliness of facilities received an 80% satisfaction rating, up 1% from the previous year. Quality of libraries received a satisfaction rating of 73%, remaining constant with the previous year. Library programs received a rating of 72%, down 1% from last year. Library materials received a rating of 72%, up 1% from the previous year. And library hours received a satisfaction rating of 62%, up 3% from the previous year. Here are the major cost factors that are included in the library's proposed 2013 financial forecast. $1.1 million for inflationary personnel costs. $500,000 covers the following items. Inflationary increase of $85,000 for materials and $12,000 for databases. IT maintenance contracts and elimination of the department's vacancy savings in the amount of $214,000. Total for the fiscal year 2013 forecast is $28.1 million. During the business planning process, the library identified four challenges that we are facing in dealing with horizon issues over the next 12 to 18 months. We will lose many experienced employees due to retirement over the next three years. We've begun to work on a succession plan to assure a smooth transition. Customers expect access to information in digital formats. However, demand for traditional library services such as hardbound materials and face-to-face assistance continues to increase at the same time. Steady growth is projected for Hispanic and Asian populations in Austin over the next 20 years. We have increased funding for Spanish language materials by 40% and world language materials by 59% to address this issue. The two core areas in which sustainability is critical to the library's future are collections and facilities. The cost of materials increases every year, and although inflationary funding has been added over the last two years, we still find ourselves in the lower quartile of public libraries, our peer public libraries. As our current 24 facilities have aged, the need for upkeep has increased accordingly. The Austin Public Library is requesting funding to address three unmet needs. Essential personnel positions. This request for $493,000 would allow the hiring of 10 essential regular budgeted positions. In 2002, the Austin Public Library had fewer staff per service hour than almost any of our peer libraries. Over those 10 years, the library lost a net of 30 positions, making it necessary to use temporary positions to maintain essential operations and keep up with increased demand in every area of the library. Every year, we use between 10 and 30 temporaries funded with vacancy savings and from other line items, such as the materials line item. This number of temps has only minimally met the department's needs. Every year, we have many more requests for temporary positions than we can afford to fund. As a result, everyone in the library works as a team to fill in wherever they occur, wherever our vacancies occur. Employees move between locations and divisions to fill in when someone is on leave or there is a vacancy. This current year, because we have few vacancies, we are leaning very heavily on the materials budget to keep the doors open and functioning and our operations functioning. This is not a sustainable staffing model. The library needs to convert these ongoing temporary positions to regular budgeted positions to just begin to address our inadequate staffing with a viable long-term solution. A dedicated budget for temporary employees. Austin Public Library has not had dedicated funding for temporary employees since fiscal year 2003. We are requesting funding in the amount of $250,000 to hire eight circulation clerks to provide direct service throughout the system. The approved funding would allow us to address staffing inadequacies and reduce the need to negatively impact other budget lines. Funding in the amount of $93,000 would provide for the addition of two custodial staff for the library. The current level of staffing is inadequate to meet the demands of cleaning 23 high-activity facilities seven days a week. The addition of these two custodians will minimize on sanitary conditions, ensuring the health and safety of our customers and staff. The library is currently involved in four ongoing CIP projects. As I mentioned before, there is growing anticipation for the new central library for the future, which will incorporate such unique elements as outdoor reading porches, rooftop garden, bicycle corral, state-of-the-art technology, and many public meeting spaces. Currently, the design development phase is underway and 60% design schematics is anticipated to be completed in September of 2012. We estimate that all exterior security cameras will be operational by the end of the fiscal year. The wastewater line replacement project at the History Center has reached the end of design development phase to be completed also by the end of the fiscal year. And the John Henry Fox Central Library boiler and flue retrofit has completed the preliminary design phase. That concludes my presentation, and I'm happy to answer any questions that you might have. Any questions? Councilor Reilly. Brenda, thanks for the presentation and for all you've been doing to provide good services with a very limited budget, and I appreciate all the constraints you've been under and everything you've been doing. I want to ask just a couple questions. First, on the whole staffing problem, you mentioned a couple times that you've been using a materials budget to keep operations going and to deal with staffing issues. I guess I hadn't realized that we were doing that with our materials budget. Now, when we look at how our materials expenditures stack up with other cities, we've seen those metrics before and we know we're not really keeping up with our peers, but when we look at that and we look at those measures, are we looking at the amount that we actually spend on materials or are we looking at the materials budget, some of which is actually going for staffing? No, we're looking at the actual materials budget, not what... The actual budget? The actual expenditures? The actual expenditures, yes. The actual expenditures don't stack up. Right. Why is it that we would have... I mean, why wouldn't we have just designated those funds for staffing positions if that was what they were going to wind up as? Why is it that we would designate it as materials and then use it for staffing? That's the only place we had any money to take. And what we do is we hold money at the beginning of the year and we only use what we absolutely have to use. We try to hold costs down, we try to hold positions vacant, but we have to have temporaries in order to keep operating. We would have to close hours if we didn't do that. Okay. On the custodial staff, you mentioned that there are 23 facilities and we're looking to hire two more staff. How many custodial staff do we currently have to cover those 23 facilities? I have that here. We currently have 13 positions for 23 facilities and we're opening 48 to 58 hours per week. So our custodial staff has spread very thin. And they deal with a lot of emergencies. So we have actually had to call people back after they've gone home to deal with some emergency situations. Okay. On the citizen survey results, I was glad to see that satisfaction with the library hours has actually gone up 3% between 2010 and 2011. I was a little surprised to see that because I know I've gotten some complaints about the hours at the Falk Library in particular. Were there other improvements? Actually, the reduced hours for John Henry Falk hadn't taken effect yet when this survey was. So we may see that in the next survey. I see. I see. So that was just a matter of timing. Right. And I assume that for purposes of the coming year, you expect to keep those same restricted hours at Falk. We're not going to be expanding any hours. And you expect that to remain the case as long as we're still in Falk? Until we open the new central. And at that time, when we open the new central, you still expect that we'll be able to go back to longer hours? Yes. Absolutely. Because we'll be having programming in the new central library and we'll have a lot of meeting spaces. We don't want to keep the restricted hours when we move to the new central. Okay. Actually, Council Member Bertland, that is Assistant City Manager for Community Services. If you recall, one of the reasons that we did do it is because based on the usage of the facility, the earlier hours were lower and the later hours were less in terms of the customers that we were serving. So it was really an operational adjustment that we made based on the usage of the facility. Plus, we also thought it would be an appropriate thing to do at this point as we start looking into moving into the new facility. Okay. There is, we did hear some complaints about matters at the FOC just recently. We had a citizen come speak at Citizens Communications, voicing concerns about some operations at the FOC. Are you aware of those concerns? And do you see any way that we're going to be able to address those concerns this coming year? And in terms of managing operations at the FOC in a different way, is there anything about this year's budget that would help us to address those concerns? Well, we're constantly looking at how to address that issue and working on it. It's not an easy issue

And then, in January, there was a DCTA presentation, and the committee asked about where to place the wheelchair in the wheelchair-accessible vehicle. And so, if you have that equipment with you, then the driver should be helping you into the vehicle and then placing it into the back for you. You also asked the additional question about the number of WAV vehicles in the fleet, and there's currently nine of those, with three more expected over the coming months. And then, the second way is that if it's on our City of Denton sidewalk work plan, so if it's not necessarily a private development area, if it's more our right-of-way, then we have a work plan for sidewalks, and it's on there. We have so much allocated each month or each year toward sidewalks. We also get some grants and other things that can kind of help us with that. And so, if there are gaps, likely our staff knows about them and it's on the sidewalk work plan. And then, if you have a specific question about a gap in it, then they'll be able to respond back to you through email and say, thanks, this is on the sidewalk work plan, or this is a new one, and we'll add it. They'll kind of be able to communicate with you what that status is. I've been contacting city staff about that section for 10 years. And I asked 10 years ago, I was told it was put on the sidewalk plan. So, how long does it take to get a sidewalk plan? So, it can take a long time, but this one, whenever we asked specifically about this segment, they said it is on the work plan, and it's a priority on the work plan. Okay. And so, you know, hopefully it'll come sooner than later. All right, thank you. Yeah. I don't know a particular answer for it. I know that our bike and pedestrian coordinator, that position has been vacant for almost a year. I think he left last summer. And so, it may be just some of the coordination there. But we can all add that to the list and just see if there's a reason. Yeah. Just like, we've got money to spend. That's good. Yeah. Right. Yeah. And some of that just goes with coordination of other projects. And so, it may be that instead of going in and doing a sidewalk and then they'd have to tear it up whenever they redo the road, it might just be waiting for the road to get redone and doing the sidewalk at the same time. So, private development is required to put in a sidewalk on their kind of property, right? And then if it's not necessarily a private developer's property, if it's city right-of-way. Council will not be taking action on these items today, and ordinance readings are tentatively scheduled for October 22nd. In compliance with statutory requirements, a draft service plan has been prepared for each area. Each service plan contains three main components. First is the Early Action Program, which lists all those services that are provided in the area commencing on the effective date of annexation. In addition, there's a list of additional services, which are those that are not required by state law for annexation but are available citywide. And then finally, there's a section that describes capital improvements that would be provided, required to provide municipal services to the area. So for item number 61, the Shaw Lane Quarry area, this includes approximately 197 acres and is located in eastern Travis County, approximately 2,225 feet south of the intersection of McKinney Falls Parkway and Shaw Lane. This area is currently in the city's ETJ and is adjacent to the city's full-purpose jurisdiction on the west side. The majority of the land in this area is owned by the city, and in addition to city-owned property, the area includes a small tract of undeveloped land on the west side of McKinney Falls Parkway, as well as a portion of McKinney Falls Parkway right-of-way, approximately 1,775 feet in length. Upon annexation, the city will provide full municipal services as described in the service plan. She currently serves as vice president for Austin Friends of Folk Art and continues to be a friend and advocate for arts, culture, and creativity in Austin. We thank you, Gloria Pennington. Thirdly, we'd like to recognize Joe Leyva. Joe Leyva of the City of Austin Building Services has provided invaluable input into the success of the Cultural Arts Division's People's Gallery Exhibition since its inception in 2005, which is located here at City Hall. He designed the permanent hanging systems that are used to install artwork along the limestone walls and which are often sought out by others as examples to emulate. During the past seven years, he has repeatedly contributed creative solutions for hanging all sorts of unique artworks within the very particular constraints of City Hall. We cannot thank Joe enough for his partnership, and though he has been promoted to a different department, we hope that he will be able to continue his participation with People's Gallery. Fourthly, we'd like to recognize Jared Neese and Claudette Godfrey. They are both with South by Southwest Film, and they donated their time and effort to partner with the City of Austin to include Faces of Austin's short film program's 2012 premiere into South by Southwest's community screening programs. The partnership will continue for 2013 premiere in March. This generous donation helps promote Austin film and filmmakers to the Austin community and beyond. Lynn Osgood. She has served with various panels, boards, and work groups, including the Art in Public Places panel, the Waller Creek Citizens Advisory Committee, the Create Austin Task Force, and most recently was appointed to the Austin Parks and Recreation Board. Her thoughtful and insightful comments as a member of the Art in Public Places panel consistently reflected her desire to see high-quality artwork that provided a meaningful contribution to both the city at large and citizens individually. It's our pleasure to have been able to work so closely with her to shape the future of Austin's public art collection, and we look forward to tapping into her extensive body of knowledge in the future. And lastly, we'd like to thank the African-American Resource Advisory Commission. This commission volunteered their time and expertise to broaden community participation in the development of artwork for the new African-American Cultural and Heritage Facility. Through their guidance and leadership, artist Reginald Adams was able to connect with a large constituency of the African-American population in East Austin, where the new facility is located, and throughout the city. Participants in the project were able to engage with the artwork in a variety of ways, including the development of the mural design, the collection of portraits of significant community leaders, and the actual making of the mural. The mural will be installed later this year, and will be welcome additions to the Art in Public Places collection. So we thank all of our organizations and individual artists for their time and talent and contribution to the arts community. Thank you. Thank you. It's very exciting, and we will be recognizing them at a luncheon on this Friday. Thank you. We'll move on to item number F, new business.

items.chapter: 4.11. COVID-19 Update
items.T0: Our drive-through testing facility at Park Plaza and other sites have done over 20,000 tests now.
items.T1: Arlington represents about 92 of those. Dallas County also slightly up. They were trending down, but now they're trending up slightly. And these are factors that we're paying attention to as we move forward. This is a seven-day rolling average, just that sort of better visualizes how we're moving. Notice the sharp spike in the midsummer. And now, this period of time, we're trending upward at a less steep incline, but we are still trending upwards. From a testing perspective, we've done a lot of testing. Our drive-through testing facility at Park Plaza and other sites have done over 20,000 tests now. Test over 2,000 people in nursing homes. Our night shelter, our life shelter, has been tested. And internally, within the public safety group, within the city of Arlington and UTA public safety, we've done about 300 antigen tests, rapid testing that we now have the testing capability to get a turnaround in about 15 minutes to determine whether or not an individual is positive. Our testing site in Park Plaza is seeing an uptick. A few weeks ago to a month and a half ago, we were around 300, 400 now. Last week, we did 738 tests.
items.T2: And Chief Krausen there, our fire department chief, is online and I think with a very comprehensive report here for us. Thank you. Thank you, Mayor. Don Krausen, fire chief, director of emergency management. And, yes, this report is a little more comprehensive because a lot of things are happening. So I'm going to share my presentation. Here we go. Hopefully it can be seen. Yes, we see it well there. Okay. Thank you. So the last 30 days, our cases have been relatively stable, no major peaks, sort of up and down, and an experience we were expecting. From a hospital perspective, we are seeing a trend up, not quite the spike we saw during the summer, but we are trending up. And the other noticeable issue is that ventilator use is also up. So these are issues of concern and we're watching very closely. From a hospitalization perspective across North Texas, COVID hospitalizations are up, particularly in Tarrant County. I've been reporting these statistics for the last five or six council meetings, and you can see that in Tarrant County, we're certainly trending up, the 419 COVID patients. Arlington represents about 92 of those. Dallas County also slightly up. They were trending down, but now they're trending up slightly. And these are factors that we're paying attention to as we move forward. This is a seven-day rolling average, just that sort of better visualizes how we're moving. Notice the sharp spike in the midsummer. And now, this period of time, we're trending upward at a less steep incline, but we are still trending upwards. From a testing perspective, we've done a lot of testing. Our drive-through testing facility at Park Plaza and other sites have done over 20,000 tests now. Test over 2,000 people in nursing homes. Our night shelter, our life shelter, has been tested. And internally, within the public safety group, within the city of Arlington and UTA public safety, we've done about 300 antigen tests, rapid testing that we now have the testing capability to get a turnaround in about 15 minutes to determine whether or not an individual is positive. Our testing site in Park Plaza is seeing an uptick. A few weeks ago to a month and a half ago, we were around 300, 400 now. Last week, we did 738 tests. So, you can see as the positive cases are increasing, our testing is going up, and we're watching all these factors very carefully as we move forward. Last seven days, we measure in several different ways, so I'm going to carry you through a number of little exercises here. There are 308 positive cases in Arlington in the last seven days. By zip code, you can still see the 76010 is the highest zip code for positives. But across the city, it's fairly well distributed, as we've indicated in the past. From an age perspective, what's notably different is now that the younger population is starting to show up at the school's opening, college opening. These are all things that we expect, not necessarily showing up in our hospitalization numbers, but all these factors and things that we have to factor in as we make decisions for the community. From an overall fatality perspective, we've remained about 18% of Tarrant County death cases. You can see that, you know, overall count, nearly 10,000, but 8,500 individuals have recovered, 125 deaths, though, in Arlington. Of that, we are very similar to the rest of the county with 94% of the deaths in Arlington coming from individuals with underlying medical conditions. Some interesting facts, though, I think, from an age perspective is that 11% of our cases are under the age of 50. 65% of our cases are over the age of 65. So knowing these factors help us adjust our strategies and helping us prepare and adjust the things we do to keep our environment stable, and we have been relatively stable. From a school district perspective, we're watching the schools very closely, and we are seeing an uptick since they've opened, but not to the degree, quite frankly, I was expecting. And I don't know if that's a good sign or not, but these are cases for concern, and we're watching these on a daily basis and tracking them with all the school districts in the city and the private schools. UTA also seeing a slight uptick, but for a large institution like this, their numbers are relatively low. We have worked with their PD department on some testing issues, and things at UTA remain relatively stable. Now, there's a cause and effect of all the things we do, and we try to track those things from holidays to special events to governor's orders, and the governor has just recently issued a new order allowing bars to operate at 50% if the local county judge authorizes that. That has occurred here, and I'll speak to that in a moment. As far as the active cases in Arlington, active case locations, we are now up to 726 active case locations. That doesn't mean that's a single individual at that location, quite frankly. Often there are numerous or multiple individuals at these locations because we believe our active individual count is probably around 1,200 or 1,300. Things are moving. The pod is in renovation right now. In fact, both the architect and the construction companies are MWBEs. We expect the facility to be completed in December, quite frankly, maybe operational by early December. Our testing site, we have a continued agreement with the state to operate through the end of October. We are now negotiating to operate that site through the end of November. As you're aware, businesses are now operating, most of them at 75%. Schools are open. We've had special events come back to life. The Cowboy game and the baseball games are all doing very well. In fact, we've had a relatively low number of concerns or complaints about COVID-related issues at the events. In fact, the first Cowboy game, I made it through the stadium, through the seats, through the suites, and checked the operation very carefully. The Cowboy organization very serious about safety, and the resulting concerns are very limited. If you've noticed the game last night at the Globe Life Field, very well managed, very careful. And I think we've proven that you can have these special events, but you have to take significant precautions to keep folks safe. And we're doing the best we can to do that, as are the team and the operators of these venues. I think the most interesting thing that's going to happen will start tomorrow. Ours will be authorized in Arlington to operate at 50%. I'll be sending out a notice to the owners and operators tomorrow, reminding them of the governor's standards and the fact that we'll be coming by to visit those establishments to ensure that they are complying with the governor's standards and working with them on that to ensure that everyone's in the right place. Now, things are moving on the vaccination front, and the fire department is now a registered entity authorized to provide vaccinations when they get here. We're operating on some fundamental assumptions that the vaccines will be here, quite frankly, by November, it looks like, or at least the information I've received. There will be some requirements. If you're going to be an entity that will do vaccinations, you have to have cold storage capability, and our refrigeration units will be here within two weeks. They are sub-zero units, and we are partnering with Tarrant County and the local hospitals to share resources as necessary. We believe the vaccine will come in two doses per individual with a separation of shots between 21 or 28 days. These are still planning assumptions. Nothing is in concrete as of yet. We will be targeting critical populations first, as the vaccines, when they come out, will be rather limited. So critical infrastructure and essential workers such as health care, EMS, pharmacy, public safety, agriculture, those types of groups will be addressed first, followed by people living in group settings, those that are incarcerated, multigenerational households, state-supported, multigenerational households, state-supported living centers, state hospitals, people experiencing homelessness, college and universities, followed by people at high risk for severe illness, nursing home residents, those over the age of 65, high-risk medical conditions, and then those with limited access to vaccination services. Certainly, the groups will be targeting as a department, and those will be the uninsured, the underserved, and those with disabilities. To do all these things, you have to be registered, and we are. You have to follow the requirements. You have to have the ability to maintain the integrity of the vaccines through cold chain requirements, and we're in position for that. You have to report the usage to the state within 24 hours, and basically track everything that you do, and we're certainly prepared for that. We have significant additional PPE to support a vaccination effort, but we would also expect that additional PPE will be provided as we step into this arena. And lastly, the generalized timeline, as we see it right now, this is simply a planning perspective, because nothing has materialized as of yet, absolutely. October, from now, October through January, we expect some limited vaccines to be here for targeted administration. We believe that January through July, we'll be able to do broad administration of the vaccine, that there is an assumption that 660 million doses will be available for the country. And then through July, through October of next year, the vaccine will be readily available with open vaccinations for basically anyone. And then October of next year, we'll be in a routine cycle where hopefully the vaccination effort will become standard like any other flu vaccine. A lot of things are changing. We're adjusting to changing winds. Our assumptions are relatively stable, but could certainly change. But we're doing the best we can to be ready for the next step. And with that, I'll go ahead and turn it back to you, Mayor and Council, for any questions. I'll stop the... Any questions for Chief Crowson? Yes, Mr. Peel? Yes, Chief. You know, I've been reading that there are multiple different vaccine variations in final development and stage three trials that are coming out. And there's now discussion that, you know, you may have three different companies with three different vaccines out there competing against each other. And that might be problematic. In your discussions with people on the timeline and the administration, I mean, have y'all discussed, are we going to get doses of vaccine A or vaccine B or vaccine C? Do you have any idea

items.chapter: 4.11. COVID-19 Update
items.T0: Our drive-through testing facility at Park Plaza and other sites have done over 20,000 tests now.
items.T1: Arlington represents about 92 of those. Dallas County also slightly up. They were trending down, but now they're trending up slightly. And these are factors that we're paying attention to as we move forward. This is a seven-day rolling average, just that sort of better visualizes how we're moving. Notice the sharp spike in the midsummer. And now, this period of time, we're trending upward at a less steep incline, but we are still trending upwards. From a testing perspective, we've done a lot of testing. Our drive-through testing facility at Park Plaza and other sites have done over 20,000 tests now. Test over 2,000 people in nursing homes. Our night shelter, our life shelter, has been tested. And internally, within the public safety group, within the city of Arlington and UTA public safety, we've done about 300 antigen tests, rapid testing that we now have the testing capability to get a turnaround in about 15 minutes to determine whether or not an individual is positive. Our testing site in Park Plaza is seeing an uptick. A few weeks ago to a month and a half ago, we were around 300, 400 now. Last week, we did 738 tests.
items.T2: And Chief Krausen there, our fire department chief, is online and I think with a very comprehensive report here for us. Thank you. Thank you, Mayor. Don Krausen, fire chief, director of emergency management. And, yes, this report is a little more comprehensive because a lot of things are happening. So I'm going to share my presentation. Here we go. Hopefully it can be seen. Yes, we see it well there. Okay. Thank you. So the last 30 days, our cases have been relatively stable, no major peaks, sort of up and down, and an experience we were expecting. From a hospital perspective, we are seeing a trend up, not quite the spike we saw during the summer, but we are trending up. And the other noticeable issue is that ventilator use is also up. So these are issues of concern and we're watching very closely. From a hospitalization perspective across North Texas, COVID hospitalizations are up, particularly in Tarrant County. I've been reporting these statistics for the last five or six council meetings, and you can see that in Tarrant County, we're certainly trending up, the 419 COVID patients. Arlington represents about 92 of those. Dallas County also slightly up. They were trending down, but now they're trending up slightly. And these are factors that we're paying attention to as we move forward. This is a seven-day rolling average, just that sort of better visualizes how we're moving. Notice the sharp spike in the midsummer. And now, this period of time, we're trending upward at a less steep incline, but we are still trending upwards. From a testing perspective, we've done a lot of testing. Our drive-through testing facility at Park Plaza and other sites have done over 20,000 tests now. Test over 2,000 people in nursing homes. Our night shelter, our life shelter, has been tested. And internally, within the public safety group, within the city of Arlington and UTA public safety, we've done about 300 antigen tests, rapid testing that we now have the testing capability to get a turnaround in about 15 minutes to determine whether or not an individual is positive. Our testing site in Park Plaza is seeing an uptick. A few weeks ago to a month and a half ago, we were around 300, 400 now. Last week, we did 738 tests. So, you can see as the positive cases are increasing, our testing is going up, and we're watching all these factors very carefully as we move forward. Last seven days, we measure in several different ways, so I'm going to carry you through a number of little exercises here. There are 308 positive cases in Arlington in the last seven days. By zip code, you can still see the 76010 is the highest zip code for positives. But across the city, it's fairly well distributed, as we've indicated in the past. From an age perspective, what's notably different is now that the younger population is starting to show up at the school's opening, college opening. These are all things that we expect, not necessarily showing up in our hospitalization numbers, but all these factors and things that we have to factor in as we make decisions for the community. From an overall fatality perspective, we've remained about 18% of Tarrant County death cases. You can see that, you know, overall count, nearly 10,000, but 8,500 individuals have recovered, 125 deaths, though, in Arlington. Of that, we are very similar to the rest of the county with 94% of the deaths in Arlington coming from individuals with underlying medical conditions. Some interesting facts, though, I think, from an age perspective is that 11% of our cases are under the age of 50. 65% of our cases are over the age of 65. So knowing these factors help us adjust our strategies and helping us prepare and adjust the things we do to keep our environment stable, and we have been relatively stable. From a school district perspective, we're watching the schools very closely, and we are seeing an uptick since they've opened, but not to the degree, quite frankly, I was expecting. And I don't know if that's a good sign or not, but these are cases for concern, and we're watching these on a daily basis and tracking them with all the school districts in the city and the private schools. UTA also seeing a slight uptick, but for a large institution like this, their numbers are relatively low. We have worked with their PD department on some testing issues, and things at UTA remain relatively stable. Now, there's a cause and effect of all the things we do, and we try to track those things from holidays to special events to governor's orders, and the governor has just recently issued a new order allowing bars to operate at 50% if the local county judge authorizes that. That has occurred here, and I'll speak to that in a moment. As far as the active cases in Arlington, active case locations, we are now up to 726 active case locations. That doesn't mean that's a single individual at that location, quite frankly. Often there are numerous or multiple individuals at these locations because we believe our active individual count is probably around 1,200 or 1,300. Things are moving. The pod is in renovation right now. In fact, both the architect and the construction companies are MWBEs. We expect the facility to be completed in December, quite frankly, maybe operational by early December. Our testing site, we have a continued agreement with the state to operate through the end of October. We are now negotiating to operate that site through the end of November. As you're aware, businesses are now operating, most of them at 75%. Schools are open. We've had special events come back to life. The Cowboy game and the baseball games are all doing very well. In fact, we've had a relatively low number of concerns or complaints about COVID-related issues at the events. In fact, the first Cowboy game, I made it through the stadium, through the seats, through the suites, and checked the operation very carefully. The Cowboy organization very serious about safety, and the resulting concerns are very limited. If you've noticed the game last night at the Globe Life Field, very well managed, very careful. And I think we've proven that you can have these special events, but you have to take significant precautions to keep folks safe. And we're doing the best we can to do that, as are the team and the operators of these venues. I think the most interesting thing that's going to happen will start tomorrow. Ours will be authorized in Arlington to operate at 50%. I'll be sending out a notice to the owners and operators tomorrow, reminding them of the governor's standards and the fact that we'll be coming by to visit those establishments to ensure that they are complying with the governor's standards and working with them on that to ensure that everyone's in the right place. Now, things are moving on the vaccination front, and the fire department is now a registered entity authorized to provide vaccinations when they get here. We're operating on some fundamental assumptions that the vaccines will be here, quite frankly, by November, it looks like, or at least the information I've received. There will be some requirements. If you're going to be an entity that will do vaccinations, you have to have cold storage capability, and our refrigeration units will be here within two weeks. They are sub-zero units, and we are partnering with Tarrant County and the local hospitals to share resources as necessary. We believe the vaccine will come in two doses per individual with a separation of shots between 21 or 28 days. These are still planning assumptions. Nothing is in concrete as of yet. We will be targeting critical populations first, as the vaccines, when they come out, will be rather limited. So critical infrastructure and essential workers such as health care, EMS, pharmacy, public safety, agriculture, those types of groups will be addressed first, followed by people living in group settings, those that are incarcerated, multigenerational households, state-supported, multigenerational households, state-supported living centers, state hospitals, people experiencing homelessness, college and universities, followed by people at high risk for severe illness, nursing home residents, those over the age of 65, high-risk medical conditions, and then those with limited access to vaccination services. Certainly, the groups will be targeting as a department, and those will be the uninsured, the underserved, and those with disabilities. To do all these things, you have to be registered, and we are. You have to follow the requirements. You have to have the ability to maintain the integrity of the vaccines through cold chain requirements, and we're in position for that. You have to report the usage to the state within 24 hours, and basically track everything that you do, and we're certainly prepared for that. We have significant additional PPE to support a vaccination effort, but we would also expect that additional PPE will be provided as we step into this arena. And lastly, the generalized timeline, as we see it right now, this is simply a planning perspective, because nothing has materialized as of yet, absolutely. October, from now, October through January, we expect some limited vaccines to be here for targeted administration. We believe that January through July, we'll be able to do broad administration of the vaccine, that there is an assumption that 660 million doses will be available for the country. And then through July, through October of next year, the vaccine will be readily available with open vaccinations for basically anyone. And then October of next year, we'll be in a routine cycle where hopefully the vaccination effort will become standard like any other flu vaccine. A lot of things are changing. We're adjusting to changing winds. Our assumptions are relatively stable, but could certainly change. But we're doing the best we can to be ready for the next step. And with that, I'll go ahead and turn it back to you, Mayor and Council, for any questions. I'll stop the... Any questions for Chief Crowson? Yes, Mr. Peel? Yes, Chief. You know, I've been reading that there are multiple different vaccine variations in final development and stage three trials that are coming out. And there's now discussion that, you know, you may have three different companies with three different vaccines out there competing against each other. And that might be problematic. In your discussions with people on the timeline and the administration, I mean, have y'all discussed, are we going to get doses of vaccine A or vaccine B or vaccine C? Do you have any idea

items.T1: Motion to second. Please vote. Jared. Motion carries. Next item is MNC 24-0085. Council Member Hill. I move that the Fort Worth City Council adopt the resolution authorizing use of the power of eminent domain to acquire .135 acres in the right-of-way easements from real property owned by Cheyenne Ridge Limited Partnership, a Texas Limited Partnership. The subject property is located at 6399 and 6398 Apache Trail in the Cheyenne Ridge addition, in addition to the City of Fort Worth, Block I-NJ, Lot 1X, Tarrant County, Texas. The land rights and the subject property are needed for the WJ Boas Road Widening Improvements Project, a public use that provides for roadway improvements including pavement reconstruction with curb and gutter, drainage improvements, street lights, charities pass, and reconstruction of the existing roundabout at Bowman Roberts Road. The property interest to be acquired is described by the meets and bounds and depicted by the survey exhibits attached as mayor and council communication. Motion a second. Please vote. Motion carries. Next item is MNC 24-0081. Motion carries.
